title: Rose on Charlie Parker: no appeal, no originality
summary: Rose says he knew and recorded Parker, studied his records closely, and still finds him unexceptional and cannot see his appeal. John notes Parker became a romantic hero of the beats.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well, it may have dramatized it to some extent, but I believe that the decline of the actualities behind the dream had already begun sometime earlier than that. I believe firmly that the American system has been in decline, demonstrably in decline, since the beginning of World War I. As far as the application of Charlie Parker, of course, I knew Charlie Parker and I didn't know Big Spider-Bank. However, it's fair to say that I know more about Big Spider-Bank than I know about Charlie Parker. In the first place, there's been infinitely more written about him. And he's been studied in much greater depth than Charlie Parker. However, I don't share, of course, the attitudes of many people about Charlie Parker's validity as an artist. And I would not have, as it were, made a study of him or his work as a result of that. I have listened extensively to Charlie Parker, both live and on records. I have studied the records, in fact, very carefully for extended periods of time just to find out if there was something I wasn't hearing that was in there. And while substantial originality is claimed for him, I never was able to discover it. And what is purported to be the jazz quality is something that I never have been able to find. And I never did know why anybody was interested in Charlie Parker as a musician, as an artist. This doesn't mean that there may be something I don't know that's happening. I have found that in many artists whose work I don't particularly enjoy, that I can nevertheless understand the basis of their appeals. But Charlie Parker, to that extent, eludes me entirely.
You don't understand the basis of his appeal?

Not at all. I don't know why anybody's interested in Charlie Parker. I could make a case for somebody being interested in Lester Young, which I'm not, but I can understand something of that. But I just can't understand it.

No, what happened with Charlie Parker is that, to a certain extent, he became a romantic hero of the beat generation. Oh, yes. Ferlinghetti, all the New York beat things. Now, the question as to why he did is somehow they read into his music a lot of protest themes. And, of course, you can take any musician's thing and read anything you wanted to it. But it's interesting that he became a kind of a basis for a romantic legend the same way Bix did. That is, in New York and Subway Walls, you'd have Bird Lives.

That's true. But as far as music is concerned, I mean, I can't understand the response of people to Mick Jagger or Alice Cooper and so on, because it is completely aesthetically meaningless to me. And I have worked with Charlie Parker and I have recorded Charlie Parker, and I have paid close and, I think, objective attention, or at least objective as much as I could be. And I found it certainly unexceptional.
